clue.text: Beautiful food, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that a word is to be taken as it is heard when spoken

parts.note: fare is food, as in the fare served at a restaurant

explanation.surface: Someone praising lovely cooking, or so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for food is FARE; said out loud it matches the spelling of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a fair maiden is a beautiful one, in the old poetic sense.

clue.text: Page checked by very severe correspondent

indicators.note: a thing checked by another is held back or restrained by it, so it is enclosed within the other word

parts.note: penal punishments are very severe ones

explanation.surface: A page boy kept in line by a harsh letter-writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a pen pal is a friend one corresponds with by letter, so a correspondent.

clue.text: Blackleg in second taxi

parts.note: a cab is a taxi

explanation.surface: A strikebreaker climbing into a second taxi.
explanation.walkthrough: A blackleg is British slang for a worker who breaks a strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a scab is a worker who crosses a picket line, exactly what a blackleg is.

clue.text: Person, for example, associated with a wine shop

parts.note: bod is informal British slang for a person

explanation.surface: Someone being given as a sample customer linked to an off-licence.
explanation.walkthrough: BOD is everyday British slang for a person, as in 'an odd bod'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish loanword: a bodega is a cellar or shop selling wine.

clue.text: Difficult: getting credit on top of loans is hard

parts.note: on tick is British slang for on credit, so tick means credit

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, taken here from loans

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Borrowing on credit when already in debt is tricky business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link setting TICK before the first letter of 'loans'; buying 'on tick' is British for buying on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a ticklish situation is a delicate, awkward or difficult one.

clue.text: Man — name sure confused hospital worker

parts.note: to man a post is to staff it

indicators.note: confused means the letters of these words are muddled into a new order

explanation.surface: A confused hospital employee who is sure about a name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a verb here; 'confused' rearranges N plus SURE into NURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: a staff nurse is a registered nurse working on a hospital ward.

clue.text: Sublime joke grasped by academic in charge

indicators.note: a thing grasped by another is held within it, so these letters go inside

parts.note: an MA, a Master of Arts, is an academic qualification and its holder
a jest is a joke

explanation.surface: A wonderful joke appreciated by a lecturer in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: something majestic is grand and awe-inspiring, which is what sublime means.

clue.text: River round York's centre in flood

indicators.note: in tells us these letters are placed inside the river's name

parts.note: the Trent is a major river in the English Midlands
O is round in shape

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, here from York's

explanation.surface: A river around the middle of York bursting its banks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trent is a major English river; O and R go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a torrent is a rushing flood of water.

clue.text: Drug I swallowed after operation

indicators.note: after places the pieces that follow it in the clue behind operation's letters

parts.note: ate means swallowed food

explanation.surface: A patient took a painkiller after surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: A category: an opiate is a drug derived from opium, such as morphine.

clue.text: Right do well after Surrey's opener dropped

indicators.note: dropped means a letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: to prosper is to do well

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, here taken from Surrey's

explanation.surface: Cricket: Surrey thrive once their opening batsman is out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' is a cricket word in the surface, but just means the first letter of Surrey; Surrey is an English county side.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: proper means right or correct, as in the proper way.

clue.text: Abruptly end holiday away

parts.note: a break is a short holiday
off means away, as in going off

explanation.surface: Cutting short a trip abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb: to break off talks is to stop them suddenly.

clue.text: What Open University offers article outlined — cut ad out

parts.note: A is the indefinite article

indicators.note: out here means not in order, so the preceding letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An editor sketching an article and trimming an advertisement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' is the anagram signal, shuffling A, OUTLINED, CUT and AD. The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university for mature students.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the Open University provides university study for grown-ups, which is learning for adults.

clue.text: Consider intentional

definitions.meaning: to weigh something up carefully, a verb

explanation.surface: Think about whether it was on purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one spelling: as a verb it means think over carefully, as an adjective planned or done on purpose.

clue.text: Join squad, English

parts.note: a unit is a squad of soldiers or police

explanation.surface: An invitation to join the England team.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to unite is to join together.

clue.text: Smash slate

definitions.meaning: to hit or shut with great force
to criticise harshly, as a reviewer might

explanation.surface: Breaking a roofing tile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slate' looks like the roofing stone but is the British verb meaning to criticise severely.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: crashing down with force, and condemning a play or film in a harsh review.

clue.text: French revolutionary leader leading honourable race

indicators.note: leading means coming in front of the next piece

parts.note: Jean-Paul Marat was a leader of the French Revolution

explanation.surface: A French revolutionary heading a respected campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' belongs with Marat, and 'leading' puts him before HON.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: a marathon is a long-distance running race.

clue.text: Fool nicking small wrench

indicators.note: nicking means stealing, so the fool takes in the small letter

parts.note: a twit is a fool

explanation.surface: An idiot pinching a little spanner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nicking' is British slang for stealing; here it means holding S inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to twist and to wrench both mean pull or turn forcibly.

clue.text: Male not in to send out carriage

indicators.note: not in says the letter is absent from the word

parts.note: to transmit is to send out a signal

explanation.surface: A man stays home rather than dispatching a coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: transit and carriage both mean the conveying of goods or people.

clue.text: Demanding firm

definitions.meaning: solid and unyielding to the touch

explanation.surface: A tough company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a company but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one adjective: a task that is difficult, and a surface that is solid.

clue.text: What to do when no longer having an axe to grind?

definitions.text: What to do when no longer having an axe to grind?

parts.words: What to do when no longer having an axe to grind?
parts.note: having an axe to grind is nursing a grievance; once it is gone, one makes peace, pictured as putting an axe into the ground

explanation.surface: Advice on what to do with a tool you no longer need to sharpen.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: making peace after a quarrel is pictured as interring a small axe, the end of a grievance.

clue.text: Permit produced by tense wife leaving gate

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: leaving means the letter departs from the word

parts.note: a wicket is a small gate

explanation.surface: A nervous wife exits through a gate with a pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' looks like an adjective about the wife but gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a ticket is a permit, such as a pass for entry or travel.

clue.text: Large hole in case presented by barrister at the end

parts.note: a crate is a packing case

indicators.note: at the end points to the final letter of barrister

explanation.surface: A lawyer presenting a big gap in a legal case at its close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks legal, matching the barrister, but is a packing box.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a crater is a large hole, as made by a bomb or meteorite.

clue.text: Uncomplimentary reviewer, a student

parts.note: a critic reviews books, films and plays
L for learner, from the L-plates of British learner drivers

explanation.surface: A student reviewer being unkind.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for a learner, from the L-plate shown by British learner drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: critical remarks are disapproving or uncomplimentary ones.

clue.text: Easy to lose head in defeat

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: slick means smooth and easy, done without effort

explanation.surface: Panicking in a loss is all too easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to lose head' sounds like panic but drops the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: to lick an opponent is to beat or defeat them.

clue.text: Constant companion of Irish playwright holding party

indicators.note: holding means the playwright's name contains the next piece

parts.note: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish dramatist
a do is a party

explanation.surface: The Irish dramatist's ever-present friend, hosting a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' is British informal for a party or celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: one's shadow follows everywhere, and a person who does so is called a shadow.

clue.text: Sign of ladies losing weight

indicators.note: losing means the letter is removed from the word

parts.note: women are ladies

explanation.surface: Dieting women showing signs of success.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: an omen is a sign of something to come.

clue.text: In hotel, immersed in a large volume

indicators.note: something immersed in another is plunged inside it, so it goes within

parts.note: a tome is a large book
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A hotel guest buried in a thick book.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: being at home is the same as being in rather than out.

clue.text: Road safety features in cases yet to be resolved

indicators.note: to be resolved means still to be sorted out, so these letters need rearranging

explanation.surface: Unsettled lawsuits about road safety measures.
explanation.walkthrough: Cat's-eyes are reflective studs set into British roads to mark lanes at night.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: these reflective studs set in the road are a safety feature that guides drivers in the dark.
